title: VIMOS image of galaxy NGC 4993 showing the visible-light counterpart to a merging neutron star pair
caption: The galaxy NGC 4993 and a kilonova, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope

recognition.text: Official ESO press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: This picture of the galaxy NGC 4993 was made with VIMOS, an instrument on ESO's Very Large Telescope at Paranal Observatory in Chile. Just above the galaxy's center, and slightly to its left, is something never seen before, the aftermath of an explosion caused by two neutron stars merging.

Neutron stars are the extremely dense collapsed cores left behind when massive stars die. When two of them spiral together and merge, the result is a rare event called a kilonova. NGC 4993 itself is not unusual. The event inside it is what makes this image special.

The merger did more than shine in visible light. It also produced gravitational waves, ripples in spacetime, and gamma rays. LIGO-Virgo detected the gravitational waves, and Fermi and INTEGRAL detected the gamma rays. The galaxy lies about 130 million light-years from Earth.
scale: NGC 4993 is about 130 million light-years from Earth, according to ESO.

understand.summary: The VIMOS instrument on ESO's Very Large Telescope observed NGC 4993 through U, R and z filters. The color mapping isn't published.
filters: 370 nm · Optical U (Very Large Telescope VIMOS)
646 nm · Optical R (Very Large Telescope VIMOS)
935 nm · Optical Z (Very Large Telescope VIMOS)
understand.eye: The galaxy and the kilonova are far too faint for the unaided eye, and the telescope gathers far more light than the eye can.

explore: VIMOS recorded the galaxy through three filters, one in ultraviolet-blue light, one in red light and one at the edge of the near-infrared. The picture is credited to A.J. Levan and N.R. Tanvir.
alt: A galaxy, with the site of a kilonova just above and slightly left of its center.
